title: The Chinese cymbal and 'Back Bay Shuffle'
summary: Leeman explains buying a 24-inch Chinese cymbal at Bill Mather's drum shop and using it on 'Back Bay Shuffle' for steady cymbal time; it became his trademark.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: Yeah, explain that to us, that Chinese cymbal thing -- everybody is involved with that thing now; Dizzy Gillespie won't even work without it.
Well, he got some of that from me, too.

I can understand it. And I want to explain to the public that this is one of the reasons, that I'm so happy to brought up the Chinese cymbal as far back as this, because nowadays, drummers, bandleaders buy Chinese cymbals so whatever drummer they have will have a Chinese cymbal, and this is a very important thing that you created man, that you started -- so please explain that to us.
Well, I was in a drum shop in New York City, a fellow who owned the drum shop was Bill Mather, he became very famous.

Well, in his drum shop, we were just discussing, he knew where he was, being there with Cozy Cole, God bless him -- but he had one of the biggest cymbals I ever saw in my life; it was a Chinese cymbal, it was 24 to 25 inches. Now this was just about in the Artie Shaw days, and I had to have that cymbal. We did that record date which I'm going back to, 'Begin the Beguine,' and one of the songs on that date was 'Back Bay Shuffle,' which was a castoff of Chick Webb -- he tried it at rehearsal, but Chick had a orchestra at that time at LaVerg, so you know the tenor saxophone, the McRat -- he wrote the arrangement.

We did 'Back Bay Shuffle' which was a big hit, on that same date, and it started off with a little thing that I developed with Chick's playing, which is a straight da-da-da, eight bars straight on the cymbal, which became a rage at that time, musically, with some musicians. Instead of a high hat, the same steady beat, you know? Even to this day, Buddy Rich starts his band off that way, on the high hats.

Then I'll get back -- all through the years, I had this big cymbal, a little piece out here, I'll have it fixed by Bill Mather, so it was playable, they had rivets in it, that's what made it sizzle. And it became more or less of a

trademark of mine. Others used it, but it also became a trademark of mine through that Artie Shaw record. I used it with Tommy Dorsey, and I used it with Charlie Barnet, and by this time, I became familiar -- now I break through this era -- that's how Ben Webster and I got to be such dear friends, was, first, he loved my cymbals.
